title: Why does Kafka retention cleanup (deleting expired log segments) cause spikes in disk I/O and temporarily degrade broker performance — deletion of many large segment files triggers metadata-heavy random I/O (inode updates, block deallocation) on top of normal sequential read/write traffic, disrupts the OS page cache (invalidated entries force consumers to read from disk), and runs in bursts (scan, batch delete, sleep, repeat) so monitoring shows periodic I/O spikes — and why is this worse on cloud disks like EBS (storage-layer amplification of delete operations)?
shortTitle: Why does Kafka retention cleanup cause spikes in disk I/O and temporarily degrade broker performance, and why is it worse on cloud disks like EBS?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka stores each partition as a series of segment files, and retention cleanup deletes whole segments once they age out by time or size. Deleting many large segment files is not free: it triggers metadata-heavy random I/O for inode updates and block deallocation, it invalidates page cache entries so subsequent consumer reads miss memory and hit disk, and the cleaner runs in periodic bursts of scan, batch delete, and sleep, so the disk I/O graph shows regular spikes that momentarily degrade broker throughput and latency. On cloud block storage such as Amazon EBS, deletes are amplified at the storage layer because the virtualized device turns a logical delete into additional backend operations, making the spikes larger and longer than on local disks.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps daily ledgers in thick bound volumes on shelves, one volume per day, and the rule is to shred volumes older than seven days. Normally clerks just write new entries and read recent volumes, which is smooth, orderly work. But once a day the shredding crew arrives and pulls dozens of old volumes off the shelves at once, updates the shelf index for each removed volume, and reclaims the empty shelf space. All that pulling, indexing, and reshelving is jerky, scattered work that ties up the aisles, and while it happens the clerks who wanted to grab a recent volume find the aisles clogged, so their lookups slow down. If the shelves are actually a rented off-site storage service rather than the branch's own room, every shred request becomes several messages back and forth to the storage company, so the disruption is bigger and lasts longer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Retention cleanup deletes big segment files in periodic bursts, and those deletes are metadata-heavy random I/O that also evict page cache, so you see spiky disk I/O and latency; on EBS the virtualized storage amplifies each delete, making it worse, which you smooth with smaller segments, staggered deletes, and headroom.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka stores each partition as a series of segment files, and retention cleanup deletes whole segments once they age out by time or size. Deleting many large segment files is not free: it triggers metadata-heavy random I/O for inode updates and block deallocation, it invalidates page cache entries so subsequent consumer reads miss memory and hit disk, and the cleaner runs in periodic bursts of scan, batch delete, and sleep, so the disk I/O graph shows regular spikes that momentarily degrade broker throughput and latency. On cloud block storage such as Amazon EBS, deletes are amplified at the storage layer because the virtualized device turns a logical delete into additional backend operations, making the spikes larger and longer than on local disks.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps daily ledgers in thick bound volumes on shelves, one volume per day, and the rule is to shred volumes older than seven days. Normally clerks just write new entries and read recent volumes, which is smooth, orderly work. But once a day the shredding crew arrives and pulls dozens of old volumes off the shelves at once, updates the shelf index for each removed volume, and reclaims the empty shelf space. All that pulling, indexing, and reshelving is jerky, scattered work that ties up the aisles, and while it happens the clerks who wanted to grab a recent volume find the aisles clogged, so their lookups slow down. If the shelves are actually a rented off-site storage service rather than the branch's own room, every shred request becomes several messages back and forth to the storage company, so the disruption is bigger and lasts longer.

**One line to remember:** Retention cleanup deletes big segment files in periodic bursts, and those deletes are metadata-heavy random I/O that also evict page cache, so you see spiky disk I/O and latency; on EBS the virtualized storage amplifies each delete, making it worse, which you smooth with smaller segments, staggered deletes, and headroom.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the file layout. A Kafka partition is a directory of log segment files, each typically up to one gigabyte by default, plus matching offset and time index files. New data is appended to the active segment sequentially, which is cheap. Retention, configured by `retention.ms` for time or `retention.bytes` for size, decides when a closed segment is too old or the partition is too large, and the cleanup process deletes whole segments, not individual records. So cleanup is fundamentally a file-deletion operation, and deleting a one-gigabyte file plus its index files has costs beyond just marking space free.

The first cost is metadata-heavy random I/O. Appending data is sequential and friendly to disks, but deleting files forces the filesystem to update inodes, free the blocks the file occupied, and update allocation metadata, which are scattered, small, random operations rather than one smooth stream. When retention removes many segments at once, the broker issues a burst of these random metadata operations on top of the steady sequential produce and consume traffic, and random I/O is far slower per operation than sequential I/O, so the disk's effective throughput for foreground work drops during the burst.

The second cost is page cache disruption. Kafka deliberately relies on the operating system page cache so that consumers reading recent data are served from memory. When a segment file is deleted, the page cache entries backing that file are invalidated and freed, and the churn of freeing and reallocating cache pages during a deletion burst reduces the cache's effectiveness for the data consumers actually want. Consumers that would have been served from memory now miss the cache and read from disk, which both slows them and adds yet more disk load precisely when the disk is already busy with deletes.

The third cost is the bursty schedule. The log cleanup thread does not trickle deletes continuously; it runs on an interval governed by `log.retention.check.interval.ms`, scanning for eligible segments, deleting a batch, then sleeping until the next cycle. This scan-delete-sleep rhythm means the I/O cost arrives in periodic spikes rather than as a smooth background load, which is exactly why monitoring shows regular saw-tooth spikes in disk utilization and latency aligned to the check interval.

Why it is worse on cloud disks like EBS comes down to storage-layer amplification. A local SSD handles a delete close to the hardware. An EBS volume is a network-attached, virtualized block device, so operations traverse a storage backend that must track and reclaim blocks across a distributed system. A delete that is one operation locally can expand into multiple backend operations, and EBS also enforces provisioned IOPS and throughput limits, so a burst of delete-driven random I/O can exhaust your IOPS budget and get throttled, stretching the spike into a longer period of degraded performance. The same burst that is a brief blip on local NVMe can become a sustained latency event on a modestly provisioned EBS volume.

The mitigations follow from the causes. You reduce segment size with `segment.bytes` or roll segments more often with `segment.ms` so each deletion removes a smaller file and the random-I/O burst per delete is smaller and more frequent rather than huge and rare, smoothing the curve. You tune `log.retention.check.interval.ms` and avoid aligning many topics to delete at the same instant, staggering retention so deletes do not all pile into one cycle across the broker. You provision cloud storage with enough IOPS and throughput headroom to absorb delete bursts, choosing a volume type and size whose baseline and burst limits comfortably exceed your steady load plus cleanup spikes. You keep spare disk capacity so cleanup is not forced to run aggressively when the disk is nearly full. And at the architecture level, tiered storage moves older segments to object storage so local deletes shrink, which both reduces local delete pressure and offloads the amplified operations from the hot block device. Here is how you tune a topic:

```bash
# Smaller segments => smaller, smoother delete bursts; staggered checks
kafka-configs.sh --alter --topic settlements --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 \
  --add-config segment.bytes=268435456,segment.ms=3600000,retention.ms=259200000
# Broker-level: how often cleanup scans (server.properties)
#   log.retention.check.interval.ms=300000
```

Senior-level nuances: this is deletion cleanup for `cleanup.policy=delete`; log compaction has its own cleaner with different but related I/O characteristics, so know which policy your topic uses. Watch the specific metrics, filesystem busy percentage, average I/O service time, and for EBS the volume queue length and burst-balance credits, because a draining burst balance is the early sign that delete bursts are exhausting your IOPS. And remember that larger segments improve steady-state append and read efficiency, so there is a trade-off: very small segments smooth deletes but add file-handle and index overhead, so you size segments to balance smooth cleanup against steady-state efficiency rather than minimizing them blindly.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs its Kafka brokers on EBS volumes. The `settlements` topic has one-gigabyte segments and three-day retention. Every few minutes the on-call dashboard showed sharp disk latency spikes, and settlement consumers briefly lagged in lockstep with them. Rajesh and Priya settlements flow through this topic.

Problem 1 — the retention cleaner woke on its interval, found several aged one-gigabyte segments across partitions, and deleted them in a batch, issuing a burst of metadata-heavy random I/O and evicting page cache, so foreground consume slowed and lag ticked up. This is the core cause: big deletes in bursts.

Problem 2 — because the volumes were EBS with a modest IOPS budget, each delete burst drained the burst-balance credits and got throttled, so the spike that would be a blip on local NVMe stretched into a visible latency event. This is the cloud-storage amplification.

Our runnable demo models a `PartitionLog` with segment files, a `RetentionCleaner` that scans, deletes a batch, and sleeps, and a `StorageDevice` abstraction with a local-SSD cost and an EBS cost that amplifies deletes and throttles on an IOPS budget. We run cleanup with large segments on EBS to show the spike, then with smaller segments and staggered checks to show it smoothed. The classes are `RetentionCleanupDemo`, `Segment`, `PartitionLog`, `RetentionCleaner`, and `StorageDevice`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a partition with eight one-gigabyte segments on an EBS volume with a modest IOPS budget, six of which have aged past retention, versus the same data stored as thirty-two smaller segments with staggered cleanup.

Step 1: During normal operation, producers append to the active segment sequentially and consumers read recent data from the page cache, so disk I/O is smooth and latency is low.

Step 2: The retention check interval fires. The cleaner scans the partition, finds six expired one-gigabyte segments, and deletes them in a single batch. Each delete issues metadata-heavy random I/O to update inodes and deallocate blocks, and all six at once is a large burst.

Step 3: Deleting those segments invalidates their page cache entries, so consumers that were being served recent data from memory now miss the cache and read from disk, adding more disk load exactly when the disk is already busy with the delete burst, and lag ticks up.

Step 4: Because this is EBS, each delete is amplified into several backend operations, and the burst drains the volume's IOPS burst balance, so the storage layer throttles I/O. The spike that would be a brief blip on local NVMe stretches into a longer latency event, and the saw-tooth pattern repeats every check interval.

Step 5: With smaller two-hundred-fifty-six-megabyte segments and staggered deletes a few per cycle, each cleanup cycle removes less data, so the random-I/O burst per cycle is small enough to stay within the IOPS budget, the cache churn is limited, and the latency stays contained. The contrast run on local NVMe shows even the large-segment burst staying within a huge IOPS budget, confirming the cloud-storage amplification is the aggravating factor.

```
  SMOOTHED:
    256MB segments + staggered deletes (few per cycle) + IOPS headroom + tiered storage
    -> small bursts within budget -> contained latency
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka stores each partition as a series of segment files and retention cleanup deletes whole segments once they age out by time or size. The reason that causes disk I/O spikes and temporary performance degradation is that deleting large segment files is not the cheap sequential work that normal appends and reads are. A delete forces metadata-heavy random I/O, updating inodes and deallocating blocks, which is scattered and slow compared to Kafka's usual sequential pattern. Deleting a segment also invalidates the page cache entries backing that file, so consumers that would have been served recent data from memory suddenly miss the cache and read from disk, adding load exactly when the disk is already busy. And the cleaner runs on an interval in a scan, batch-delete, sleep rhythm, so the cost arrives in periodic bursts, which is why monitoring shows a regular saw-tooth of disk utilization and latency rather than a smooth line.

On cloud block storage like EBS this is worse because of storage-layer amplification. An EBS volume is a network-attached virtualized device, so a delete that is nearly free on local hardware expands into multiple backend operations, and EBS enforces provisioned IOPS and throughput limits. A burst of delete-driven random I/O can drain the volume's burst balance and get throttled, so the brief blip you would see on local NVMe stretches into a sustained latency event on a modestly provisioned EBS volume.

On the National Bank of India brokers, which run on EBS, we saw settlement latency and consumer lag spike every few minutes in lockstep with the retention check interval, because the cleaner was deleting several one-gigabyte segments at once and exhausting the volume's IOPS budget. The fixes we applied map directly onto the causes. We reduced the segment size so each delete removes a smaller file and the random-I/O burst is smaller and more frequent rather than huge and rare, which smooths the curve. We staggered retention so not every topic deletes in the same cycle, and we tuned the check interval. We provisioned the EBS volumes with enough IOPS and throughput headroom to absorb delete bursts, kept spare disk capacity so cleanup never runs in a panic near a full disk, and adopted tiered storage so older segments live in object storage and local deletes shrink.

The nuances I always mention are that this is the delete cleanup policy specifically, that compaction has its own cleaner with related but different I/O, and that I watch the right signals, filesystem service time and queue length and, on EBS, the burst-balance credits, because a draining burst balance is the early warning that delete bursts are outrunning the IOPS budget. I also point out the trade-off, since larger segments are more efficient for steady-state appends and reads, so I size segments to balance smooth cleanup against steady-state efficiency rather than making them as small as possible. The one-line principle is that retention cleanup is real, bursty, random disk work layered on top of smooth sequential traffic, and on virtualized cloud disks it is amplified, so you engineer for the spike rather than being surprised by it.

keyPoints: Retention: time-based (7 days default) or size-based
Compaction: keep latest value per key — delete old versions
Compacted topic: acts as a key-value snapshot store
